title: Why Does Church Membership Still Matter?
subtitle: Not a building you sample, not a service you rate, but a body you bind yourself to. A Christian reckoning with committed membership in a local church against the consumer church-hopping of the age, with covenant and accountability, and with the cost and the gift of belonging to imperfect people you did not choose.

connections.label: Membership is belonging to the family of God made concrete and accountable. The church as family has its own page.
The vow to stay is the cure for the consumer faith that shops and leaves. Consumer faith and the communal church has its own page.
Committed belonging is the soil where the one-anothers can actually be obeyed. Life together has its own page.
Membership is not an add-on to following Jesus but part of what it means. Discipleship has its own page.
Staying in a flawed body is where reconciliation is learned and practiced. Conflict and reconciliation has its own page.

parts.title: The Year You Did Not Stay
parts.body:
You have left a church before, and you can still feel the reasons. The music turned a direction you did not love. The new pastor preached longer and warmer than the old one, or shorter and colder. Someone said a thing in a meeting that landed wrong, and you went home and felt the small click of a door closing inside you. A better congregation opened across town, with a parking lot that worked and a youth program your kids liked, and the move felt less like leaving a family than upgrading a subscription. You did not agonize over it. You just stopped going, and then you went somewhere else, and almost no one from the first place ever called to ask where you went.

That is the strange freedom the age has handed every believer. You can belong to a church the way you belong to a gym, comparing the offerings, weighing the convenience, staying as long as it serves you and leaving the moment it disappoints, and nothing about the arrangement asks more of you than your attendance. You are a customer with a faith, and the church is a vendor of religious goods, and the whole transaction is so reasonable, so frictionless, so much like everything else you choose and discard in a consumer life, that it never occurs to you there might be another way to belong to a people.

Let me name the thing I told myself for years, because it sounds like wisdom and it is not. I told myself I was keeping my options open. That commitment to a particular flawed congregation was naive, that the mature move was to stay free, attend lightly, and reserve the right to walk when the place stopped meeting my needs. So I never joined. I never bound myself. I attended three churches in five years and was a stranger in all of them, known by no one, accountable to no one, free as a leaf in the wind, and just as rooted, and I called my rootlessness discernment.

Here is what the church-hopping life does to a soul, slowly. It teaches you that belonging is conditional, that other Christians are interchangeable, that the answer to disappointment is exit rather than repair. So you never stay anywhere long enough to be truly known, which means you are never truly held, which means that when the hard season comes, and it always comes, there is no body that has covenanted to walk through it with you, only a series of places you used to attend. You have spread yourself across many congregations and put down roots in none, and you cannot understand why your faith feels so portable and so thin.

We built a Christianity you can leave without anyone noticing, and then we wondered why no one felt they belonged. We taught a generation that the local church is optional and that commitment is a trap, and then we grieved that they would not commit. The restless believer drifting from church to church, sampling and exiting, never bound and never held, is not a free spirit who has outgrown the need for a people. He is a homesick child who has been told the door is always open and has never once been asked to come inside and stay.

parts.title: Why the Vow to Stay Is Not Optional
parts.body:
It matters because the love the New Testament commands cannot be practiced by a person who reserves the right to leave. The letters are full of one-another commands, bear one another's burdens, forgive one another, confess your sins to one another, and every one of them assumes a fixed and known one another, a particular body of people you have bound yourself to over time. You cannot bear the burdens of a congregation you are sampling. You cannot forgive a brother you can simply replace. The love of the New Testament is covenant love, the love that stays, and a Christianity organized around the freedom to exit has quietly made that love impossible while keeping its vocabulary.

It matters because you are not sanctified by the people you choose but by the people you are stuck with. The consumer leaves the moment the friction starts, and so he never gets sanded, never learns the patience that only grows in the company of the difficult, never has to forgive because he can always relocate. The member stays, and the staying is the school. The irritating elder, the family whose theology grates, the brother who failed you, are not reasons to find a better church. They are the very instruments God means to use, the iron that sharpens iron only by contact, and the believer who keeps leaving to escape the friction keeps escaping the thing God was using to make him holy.

It matters because the church-hopping faith has produced exactly the rootless, anxious, unaccountable Christian the surrounding culture already manufactures by the million, and that is the opposite of what the church was for. The world cannot stop moving, cannot stay, cannot commit, treats every bond as provisional and every belonging as exitable, and a church that simply baptizes that restlessness has nothing to offer a man drowning in his own freedom. The committed local body is a sign held up against the age, a people who have promised to stay, and when the church learns to leave as easily as everyone else, it withholds from a homeless world the one thing it most needed to see, that there is a kind of belonging you cannot lose by disappointing it.

And it matters because the watching skeptic reads our commitment to one another as the proof or the disproof of everything we say about a God who keeps covenant. We preach a God who will never leave us nor forsake us, who binds himself to a people who fail him, who stays. And then the skeptic watches us leave a congregation over the music, drop a brother who let us down, treat the body of Christ like a service we are free to cancel, and he draws the obvious conclusion, that our belonging is as conditional as anyone's and our God, if he is like his people, is the kind who leaves. The vow to stay is not a private discipline. It is a public sermon about the faithfulness of God, and the church-hopping life preaches that sermon false.

parts.title: What Scripture Means by Belonging to a Body
parts.body:
Scripture knows nothing of the unattached believer who follows Jesus while floating free of any particular church. From the first chapters of Acts the picture is fixed and concrete. The three thousand who believed at Pentecost did not scatter into private spiritualities. They devoted themselves to the apostles teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers, and they were together and had all things in common, day by day attending the temple and breaking bread in their homes. The verb is devoted. They bound themselves. The earliest Christian belonging was not attendance at an event but membership in a shared and daily life, a defined body of people who knew one another well enough to share their possessions and their meals and their burdens.

The one-another commands are the clearest proof that Scripture assumes a committed body, because every one of them requires a known and stable community to be obeyed at all. Love one another, the command runs through the whole New Testament, and beside it bear one another's burdens, forgive one another, be kind to one another, confess your sins to one another, encourage one another, do not give up meeting together. Read them slowly and notice what they require. You cannot bear a burden you do not know about, cannot forgive a brother you have already left, cannot confess to people who are gone next month, cannot encourage a stranger you nod at. The one-anothers are not suggestions for a crowd. They are the obligations of a family, and they presuppose exactly the kind of fixed, committed, mutually known belonging that the consumer faith has dissolved.

Paul gives that belonging its definitive shape when he calls the church a body, and the metaphor is fatal to the detachable Christian. The body is one and has many members, and the members do not get to leave. The eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you, and the foot does not get to resign because it is not the eye. If one member suffers, all suffer together, if one is honored, all rejoice together. Paul is writing to a divided, individualistic church and demolishing the very idea that a believer is a free agent who occasionally associates with others. You are a member, a body part, organically joined to the rest, and a body part that detaches itself does not become independent. It dies. The hand that leaves the body is not liberated. It is a corpse.

The New Testament also assumes that belonging is accountable, marked, and led, not a vague and private feeling. There are elders who keep watch over souls and will give an account, and the writer of Hebrews tells the people to obey their leaders and submit to them, which means the people knew exactly whose leaders they were. There is discipline, the painful capacity of a body to name sin and, in the worst case, to put a member outside, which only makes sense if there was an inside, a defined membership with a real edge. There are lists, the widows enrolled and cared for, the church keeping track of its own. Belonging in Scripture has a door you walk through and a body that can hold you to your place, because love that cannot be counted on is not yet the love the New Testament means.

And underneath all of it runs the language of covenant, which is the deepest word Scripture has for how God binds himself to a people and how a people binds itself in return. God does not relate to us through a series of cancellable arrangements. He cuts covenant, binds himself by oath, promises to be our God and to make us his people, and stays bound even when we break faith. The church is the covenant community, the people of the new covenant in the blood of Christ, and to belong to it is to be drawn into a faithfulness that is not first ours but his. Committed membership in a local body is not a human invention laid over a private faith. It is the shape that covenant takes on the ground, a people who have bound themselves to one another because they have first been bound, unbreakably, by the God who keeps covenant to a thousand generations and never once treats his people as a service he is free to cancel.

parts.title: How the Church Bound Itself Together
parts.body:
The early church drew a real and costly line around belonging, because in a hostile world it had to. To be baptized into the church was to leave one world and enter another, and the early Christians took the entering with enormous seriousness. The catechumens were instructed for as long as three years before baptism, examined in their lives and not only their doctrine, and only then admitted to the table. Membership was no casual association. It could cost you your standing, your family, sometimes your life, and a people who paid that much to belong did not treat belonging as a thing you sampled and discarded. They knew exactly who was inside the body, because being inside the body had become the central fact of their lives.

Cyprian, the bishop of Carthage who would die a martyr in 258, gave this its sharpest ancient expression in his treatise on the unity of the church, written while a persecution was tearing congregations apart and some were breaking away to form rival bodies. He insisted that you cannot have God as your Father if you will not have the church as your mother, that the believer who tears himself from the body cuts himself off from the life that flows only through it. He pictured the church as a single seamless garment, a single body that schism murders. His words can be pressed too hard, and later centuries did press them into cruelties he never meant. But the core of it stands as a rebuke to every age that treats the church as optional. Cyprian could not conceive of a Christian who belonged to Christ while refusing to belong, really and accountably, to Christ's people.

The monastic movement carried committed belonging into its most deliberate form, the vow of stability. When Benedict wrote his Rule in the sixth century, he required of every monk a promise to remain in one community for life, and he reserved his harshest words for the gyrovagues, the wandering monks who drifted from house to house, always moving, never submitting, slaves to their own restlessness and their own appetites, never staying anywhere long enough to be corrected or known. Benedict understood that the wandering itself was the spiritual disease, that you cannot be formed by a community you can always leave, and that the vow to stay in one ordinary, imperfect, irritating house of brothers was the very crucible God would use to make a soul. The monastery was an experiment in the conviction that holiness requires roots.

The Reformation and the Free Church traditions that followed gave the church the explicit covenant. The Anabaptists, then the English Separatists and the Congregationalists, bound their churches together by written covenants, solemn promises in which believers pledged before God to walk together as a people, to watch over one another, to submit to mutual discipline, to bear one another's burdens, and not to forsake the body. The Salem covenant of 1629 was a single sentence in which a people gave themselves up to the Lord and to one another to walk together in all his ways. The Baptists made the church covenant central to congregational life, and many of those covenants are still read aloud at the front of old church manuals, plain and searching documents in which a believer promises to strive for the advancement of this church, to participate in its worship and its sorrows, and not to forsake the assembling of ourselves together. Membership, in this tradition, was a vow, not a preference.

And the modern story is the slow unraveling of all of it, which we are living now. As Western society grew richer, more mobile, and more individualistic, the covenant quietly became a customer relationship. The automobile let a family drive past three faithful churches to the one with the better program. The consumer logic of the wider culture seeped into the pew until choosing a congregation became indistinguishable from choosing a brand and church membership, once a serious and binding covenant, became a loose association you could enter and exit without anyone marking it. The wisest voice of the last century saw it coming. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, who built an underground seminary at Finkenwalde and wrote Life Together out of that fragile experiment in Christian community under the shadow of the Reich, warned that the believer who loves his dream of community more than the actual broken community in front of him will destroy both. We do not get to construct the church we wish we had. We receive the church we are given, flawed people bound together by Christ alone, and Bonhoeffer knew that the consumer who keeps shopping for a better body is really running from the only kind of church that has ever existed, the kind made of sinners, the kind you have to forgive in order to stay.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: The human dynamics of commitment, belonging, and exit have been studied closely by sociologists, economists, and psychologists, and much of what they have found is true and illuminates exactly what the consumer church has lost. All truth is God's truth, and the church can learn from honest observers of how people bind themselves to groups or fail to. But every account of commitment carries a buried picture of what a person is and what belonging is finally for, and that picture has to be tested. What follows takes several bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each sees clearly, and weighs each against Scripture.

secular.author: Albert O. Hirschman
secular.whatItGetsRight: Hirschman, writing in 1970, drew the lasting distinction between two responses to a failing institution. You can exit, simply leave and take your business elsewhere, or you can use voice, stay and work for repair from within. He showed that the easy availability of exit actually weakens institutions, because the members most able to improve a place are the first to leave when they can, draining away the very people whose voice might have healed it. Loyalty, he argued, is what holds a person in long enough for voice to do its slow work. This describes the consumer church with eerie precision, the believer who exits at the first disappointment and so never stays to repair what is broken.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Hirschman frames loyalty as a useful brake on exit, valued because it helps institutions function better. Scripture goes deeper and calls the staying covenant, not strategy. The believer does not remain in a flawed church because staying produces better organizational outcomes but because he is bound by a vow that images the faithfulness of a God who keeps covenant with a people who fail him. Hirschman can explain why exit harms a body. Only Scripture explains why a Christian forfeits the right to it, having been joined to a body he no longer owns, and gives the power to stay when staying costs more than leaving ever would.

secular.source: Bowling Alone and the collapse of social capital
secular.author: Robert Putnam
secular.whatItGetsRight: Putnam documented with overwhelming evidence that Americans have grown dramatically more disconnected over recent decades, that the committed memberships which once wove people together, the lodges, unions, leagues, and congregations, have thinned out, and that this collapse carries real costs to health, trust, and civic life. He showed that human beings need thick, committed, long-term belonging, that loose and provisional association cannot substitute for it, and that the decline of binding membership is a genuine social catastrophe. He found religious congregations to be among the strongest remaining sources of the very commitment people are starving for.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Putnam treats committed membership chiefly as social capital, an asset valued for what it produces for the individual and the society. Scripture treats belonging to a body not as a useful asset but as part of what a human being is, a member made for a body, an image bearer of a God who is himself a communion. Our rootlessness is not merely inefficient. It is a violation of our nature and, beneath that, a refusal of the people God has bound us to. The research proves we are withering without committed belonging. Only the gospel explains why and gives back a belonging that is covenant rather than convenience.

secular.author: Barry Schwartz
secular.whatItGetsRight: Schwartz demonstrated that the endless options of consumer culture, far from liberating us, tend to paralyze and dissatisfy, that people with too many choices commit to none of them, second-guess the ones they make, and remain restlessly convinced that something better is just out of reach. This is a precise diagnosis of the church-hopper, kept perpetually unsettled by the suspicion that a better congregation exists across town, unable to commit because commitment forecloses the other options, and miserable in exactly the freedom that was supposed to satisfy.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Schwartz shows that unlimited choice corrodes commitment and offers, at most, the advice to choose less and settle more for your own well-being. Scripture reframes the whole situation. The believer is not finally a chooser surveying options at all but a member who has been chosen and placed, joined to a body by God before he ever shopped for one. The cure for the paralysis of choice is not a better technique of choosing but a different identity, the discovery that you belong to a people you did not select and may not return, and that this givenness, far from a loss of freedom, is the ground on which a settled and unanxious life can finally be built.

secular.source: Theories of liquid modernity and the disposable bond
secular.author: Zygmunt Bauman
secular.whatItGetsRight: Bauman described with great force how modern life turns everything, including our deepest relationships and communities, into loosely held arrangements to be kept while satisfying and discarded when not, so that people approach even their most important bonds as provisional and exitable. This is an exact portrait of the consumer church, the believer who holds his congregation lightly, ready to leave the moment it disappoints, and the critique names the corrosive effect of treating covenant belonging as a disposable product.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Bauman exposes the disposable self with brilliance and offers no power to escape it, only a sharp picture of the cage. Scripture not only names the disease but provides the cure, a belonging that is not held lightly and dropped but received and kept, a covenant membership in a body you do not get to discard when it fails you. The gospel breaks the liquid self not by better critique but by a new identity, you are not a customer free to cancel but a member bought with a price and joined to a body for good. The thinker can show you the trap. Only Christ unbinds you from it, by binding you, unbreakably, to his people.

secular.source: The research on commitment and relationship stability
secular.author: Caryl Rusbult and relationship scientists
secular.whatItGetsRight: The investment model of commitment, developed through decades of careful research, found that people stay in relationships not chiefly through fleeting satisfaction but through commitment, which is built by investment, by the things you have poured in that you would lose by leaving, and by the deliberate devaluing of alternatives. The studies show that lasting bonds depend on people stopping the comparison, ceasing to scan for something better, and binding themselves through accumulated, irreversible investment. This describes precisely why the church-hopper never bonds, never investing enough to make leaving costly, always keeping the alternatives in view.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The research illuminates the mechanics of how commitment forms and frames it as a calculation of investments and alternatives, a self managing its own attachments for its own stability. Scripture grounds commitment somewhere deeper than a favorable balance of investment. The believer stays not because he has invested too much to leave but because he has been claimed, bound by a covenant that does not depend on his running tally of costs and benefits. The science can describe why the rooted are stable and the rootless are not. Only the gospel supplies a commitment that holds when the investment seems lost and the alternatives look better, because its anchor is not the self's calculation but the faithfulness of God.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Believers who share the same Scripture and the same conviction that the church is a body to be committed to still disagree about how that commitment should be marked and structured, and the disagreement is serious and old. It runs to whether real belonging requires a formal covenant membership or is better marked by deep, committed, but informal belonging. Hear each view at its strongest, because both are trying to honor the same body, and both are guarding against a real danger.

views.view: Belonging should be sealed by formal covenant membership
views.body: This view holds that real commitment must be made concrete, marked, and accountable, and that the church should bind its members through a formal covenant, a public promise in which a believer joins a particular body, submits to its elders, and accepts responsibility for its life and discipline. Without such a marked door, this view argues, belonging quietly dissolves into the very consumerism that is hollowing the church out, where people attend without committing and leave without consequence. Advocates point to the seriousness with which the New Testament treats membership in the body, to the discipline the apostles expected congregations to exercise, which assumes a defined edge between inside and out, to the elders who keep watch over named souls, and to the long covenant tradition of the Free Churches, where believers solemnly promised before God to walk together and not to forsake the assembly. They argue that you cannot bear one another's burdens or watch over one another's souls without knowing exactly who the one another is, and that a body with no defined membership is not a family but a crowd. The danger they are guarding against is real and visible everywhere, a borderless Christianity where no one is committed, no one is accountable, the discipline of the church becomes impossible because no one has agreed to be under it, and the lonely consumer drifts at the edges forever, never bound, never held, free to vanish the moment he is challenged. Against that, they hold that the family of God should be entered through a real and public door, that membership is a covenant and not a formality, and that the love and accountability Scripture commands can only be practiced among people who have actually, formally, and lastingly bound themselves to one another.

views.view: Belonging is sealed by committed shared life more than formal structure
views.body: This view agrees the church is a body to be committed to and warns that formal membership can become a hollow substitute for the real thing, a name on a roll that certifies belonging while the person remains, in fact, a stranger. It points to the early church, where belonging was marked first not by a register but by a shared life, by people who broke bread together daily, bore each other's burdens, and stayed through the cost, and it argues that the deepest commitment is relational before it is institutional. A person can be a formal member of a congregation and utterly unknown within it, this view notes, and a person can be woven so deeply into the committed life of a body, present in every hard hour, accountable to real friends, rooted past the point of easy exit, that the absence of paperwork changes nothing real. Advocates point to Jesus, who defined his family not by a roll but by doing the will of God together, and to the danger that an over-formalized church can mistake the structure for the substance, counting members while love grows cold and the inactive name on the list outnumbers the living disciple. The danger they are guarding against is also real, a church that has confused belonging with bureaucracy, that processes people into membership and never actually brings them into the family, where the lonely are on the roll and still alone, and where the covenant signed becomes a thing checked off rather than a life shared. Against that, they hold that the mark of real commitment is a shared and accountable life, that the test of whether you belong is whether you are known and knowing, bearing and borne, present when it costs, and that the church must guard against letting a formal structure stand in for the costly, rooted, daily belonging that actually makes a body a family.

parts.title: What the Vow to Stay Forms in You
parts.body:
You cannot bind yourself to a flawed and demanding local church without being changed by it, and the change is exactly the kind that the church-hopping life can never produce. The believer who keeps leaving stays the same for years because nothing is allowed to rub against him long enough to wear anything down. The one who takes the vow to stay gets sanded, and God, who knew this when he saved you into a covenant people rather than into a private and portable faith, means the very staying to be the chief instrument of your formation.

It forms in you a faithfulness that mirrors the faithfulness of God, which is the deepest thing a creature can be taught. The consumer learns that bonds are provisional and that disappointment justifies exit. The member learns the opposite, in his own body, over years, that you can stay through the disappointment, keep faith with people who have failed you, refuse to leave when leaving would be easy and defensible, and that this staying is what covenant means. A person who has kept faith with one ordinary congregation through a hard decade comes out the far side knowing in his bones what it is to be bound to people who do not deserve it, which is the only way a creature ever begins to understand how God has stayed bound to him.

It forms patience and the long capacity to forgive, because you cannot stay in a body long without being wounded and without wounding, and the staying is the school the wound is meant for. The hopper leaves when hurt and so never learns to forgive, only to relocate. The member stays, addresses it, bears the offense, extends the grace, and learns in the friction the patience that does not insist on its own way and the forgiveness that releases a debt. Every difficult brother who does not drive him out becomes an occasion to practice the love that endures, and a believer who has stayed through real offenses comes out gentler, slower to take offense, harder to drive off, more like the One who has borne with him through far worse.

It forms humility, because submitting to a particular body and its leaders is a steady death to the sovereign consumer self that answers to no one. The hopper is accountable to nobody, free to design his own faith, correct only by his own lights, because he has placed himself above every congregation by reserving the right to leave them all. The member lays that sovereignty down. He accepts that he is one part of a body and not the whole, that he can be told he is wrong by people who have a claim on him, that his preferences do not rule and his judgment is not final, and the long submission cures him of the quiet pride of the man who has made himself the only authority over his own soul.

And it forms in you a foretaste of the belonging that has no end, which is the formation beneath all the others. The end of the whole story is not a private heaven of unattached souls but a city, a wedding feast, a countless multitude bound together as one people around the throne, the covenant complete and unbreakable at last. The church-hopping faith is training for nothing, because there will be no exit there, no shopping, no better body across town. But the believer who has learned to stay, to bind himself, to keep faith with a flawed and beloved people through all the years and all the disappointments, is being trained week by week for that, his restless heart slowly enlarged to the shape of a belonging he will never want to leave and never be able to lose, already tasting, in the costly faithfulness of the vow to stay, the thing he was made for and will one day have in full.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: The vow to stay is not made by feeling committed. It is made by small, concrete, repeated acts of binding yourself and refusing the exit, over years, under grace. None of what follows will turn a hopper into a rooted member overnight, and that is not how roots are grown. They are grown by staying through the seasons that tempt you to leave. Begin with one thing, this week, and let the rest come as you put down roots that would cost you something to tear up.

steps: Name honestly, before God, the real reason you left the last church you left, and whether it was a matter worth leaving over or simply a disappointment you could have stayed through. The first step toward the vow to stay is seeing how easily you have broken it.

Pray this week for the church you are part of, by name, the flawed and ordinary one in front of you and not the ideal one in your head, and ask God to make you a member of it rather than a consumer of it.

Resist the scan for something better. This week, when the thought rises that a different congregation might suit you more, notice it and set it down, the way Schwartz says the only path out of restless dissatisfaction begins, by ceasing to compare.

Have one conversation that ties you a little tighter to the body where you are, with a person whose name you will keep. Belonging deepens by knowing and being known, and the vow to stay grows out of relationships you would grieve to leave.

Commit to one church and stop shopping. Decide, before God, that this ordinary body is your people now and that you will stay through the disappointments that will surely come, the way you stay in a family. The settled refusal to keep looking is where the vow begins.

Read your church's covenant or statement of membership if it has one, slowly, as a vow and not a formality, and weigh what it would mean to actually keep every line. If your church has no such covenant, find an old one and let its searching promises show you what binding belonging once meant.

Move from the back to the body. Join one smaller gathering below the size where you can hide, where you can be known and held and missed, and let yourself be folded into a part of the church that would notice if you were gone.

Bear one burden in the body that ties you to it. Bring the meal, give the ride, sit with the grieving, and feel how serving a particular people begins to make leaving them unthinkable. You become a member by carrying weight, not by evaluating sermons.

Take the formal step into membership if your church offers it, and make your belonging concrete, marked, and accountable rather than vague and exitable. Let yourself be claimed by a body and held to your place, and treat the covenant as a vow before God and not a card in a file.

Submit to the leadership God has placed over you in a real and costly matter, accepting correction or counsel from someone with a claim on your soul. The long death of the sovereign consumer self begins the first time you let a brother tell you that you are wrong and you do not leave.

Stay through one disappointment that tempts you to exit. Something or someone will fail you this season, because bodies are made of sinners. Stay, address it, forgive, and let the staying teach you the faithfulness the hopper never learns. The wound borne in love is how roots go deep.

Open your home and your table to the body the way the early Christians did, glad and generous and regular, without an agenda. The covenant people of God are bound together around tables as much as pulpits, and a church you eat with becomes a church you cannot easily leave.

Put down roots deep enough that leaving would cost you, and treat that cost as a sign of health rather than a problem to escape. The believer who can leave painlessly never belonged. Stay somewhere long enough that the people become, truly and irreversibly, your family.

Become a member the church relies on, the one who shows up for the funerals and the moves and the hospital rooms, the one whose faithfulness the body has learned to count on through the long, unglamorous years. A covenant member is known by his reliability in the hard decades, not his attendance in the easy months.

Take in the church-hopper the way someone should have taken you in. Watch for the visitor who slips out early, the restless one comparing congregations, the soul who cannot commit, and bring him into the family and show him, by your own staying, that there is a kind of belonging you do not have to lose by disappointing it.

Let the vow to stay form you, over a lifetime, into someone fit for the belonging that has no end. Stay, love, submit, forgive, and bear, through all the seasons that tempt you to leave, until the costly faithfulness of one ordinary covenant has enlarged your heart to the shape of the great covenant it images, the unbreakable belonging of the people of God gathered as one around the throne, where no one shops and no one leaves and the family of God is finally, fully home.

kicker: Church Membership and the Vow to Stay
